clue.text: Accompanied by employer for the prosecution

definitions.note: a phrase standing for the one who is for the prosecution

blocks.note: acc. is the abbreviation for accompanied, as in music
one who employs something uses it

explanation.surface: A lawyer appears in court alongside the boss, who is giving evidence for the prosecution.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a phrase: the person who speaks for the prosecution in a case.
explanation.definitionFit: The one who brings a charge against someone stands on the prosecuting side of a trial.

clue.text: Fall for 26 by 10

definitions.note: the subject of Keats's poem To Autumn

blocks.note: first meaning: the American word for the season after summer
second meaning: the season addressed in a famous ode by the puzzle's poet

explanation.walkthrough: '26 by 10' is an ode by John Keats; his ode To Autumn begins 'Season of mists and mellow fruitfulness'.
explanation.definitionFit: Fall is the American name for the same season, and Keats addressed his ode to that season.

clue.text: Light for Eric and Leslie

indicators.note: the answer is held for us within the run of names that follows

blocks.note: running across the end of the first name, the conjunction and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A lamp is being provided for two men called Eric and Leslie.
explanation.definitionFit: A wax stick with a wick burns to give illumination, so it is a source of light.

clue.text: Back member of Lloyd's initialled by American

blocks.note: to back a proposal is to second it
the private backers of the Lloyd's insurance market are called Names

explanation.surface: An American signs off his initials on the support of a Lloyd's underwriter.
explanation.walkthrough: Lloyd's of London is the insurance market whose investors are called Names. Americans habitually give a middle name as an initial, as in John F. Kennedy.
explanation.definitionFit: The middle name is the one an American usually reduces to an initial between the first name and surname.

clue.text: H-half open up for the prince

indicators.note: in a down light, 'up' means the letters are read from the bottom upward

blocks.note: the letter itself, standing alone with its stutter
a door left ajar is half open

explanation.surface: Someone stammers a request to open up for a royal visitor.
explanation.walkthrough: The stutter 'H-half' looks like one word; it supplies the letter H and then 'half open'.
explanation.definitionFit: A rajah is an Indian prince or king, the title being the Hindi for ruler.

clue.text: A time for little boy to be like a ...

definitions.note: the dots run on into 9 across: like a tonic with bubbles

blocks.note: taken as written
an era is a period of time
Ted is a short boy's name, a pet form of Edward

explanation.surface: A small boy is told to behave like something, the sentence trailing off to be finished by the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The dots join this clue to 9 across, so the phrase reads like a fizzy tonic: aerated tonic water.
explanation.definitionFit: Tonic water is charged with gas bubbles, so being fizzy like it means being charged with air.

clue.text: The last reformer, an English king

indicators.note: a reformer remakes things, so these letters are formed afresh

blocks.note: the letters of both words together
taken as written

explanation.surface: The final reformer is said to have been an English monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: Athelstan was the tenth-century king of the West Saxons, often called the first king of all England.
explanation.definitionFit: Athelstan ruled in the 920s and 930s, the first to rule the whole English realm.

clue.text: He did naughty things in the garden shed

definitions.note: the second definition is a place-phrase: a thing found in the garden shed

blocks.note: first meaning: a dissolute man of loose morals
second meaning: a long-handled tool with teeth kept with the gardening tools

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests misbehaviour in a shed; really it is a libertine on one side and a garden tool on the other.
explanation.definitionFit: A rake is a dissolute pleasure-seeker, and also the toothed tool for gathering leaves kept with gardening kit.

clue.text: Girl with a cat, awfully sad

indicators.note: done awfully means done badly, so the letters are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A girl with her cat looks very sad.
explanation.definitionFit: Tragical is an old or poetic form meaning tragic, sorrowful and distressing.

clue.text: Norfolk town, always separate

blocks.note: Diss is a market town in Norfolk, in the east of England
ever means at all times

explanation.surface: A Norfolk town is forever split apart.
explanation.definitionFit: To dissever is to cut apart or divide, a formal verb meaning to sever.

clue.text: ... bracing note

blocks.note: first meaning: invigorating, like a pick-me-up
second meaning: the keynote of a musical scale

explanation.walkthrough: The dots continue 5 across, so the run reads like an aerated tonic; on its own this clue is two meanings of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: A restorative medicine or drink braces you up, and in music the first degree of the scale is called this.

clue.text: Writer of other than jokes

indicators.note: 'other' asks for the following words made into something different, a fresh arrangement

blocks.note: the letters of both words together

explanation.surface: A writer of anything other than jokes: a serious author.
explanation.walkthrough: The poet John Keats is the theme of the puzzle; his odes and poems fill many of the other lights.
explanation.definitionFit: Keats was an English Romantic poet, so he is a writer of verse.

clue.text: George, writer on music and film, retains endless security with 26 by 10

definitions.note: the subject of Keats's Ode on Melancholy

indicators.note: something without an end has lost its final letter
to retain is to hold something inside oneself

blocks.clueFragment: George, writer on music and film
blocks.note: George Melly, jazz singer who also wrote on music and reviewed films
an anchor gives security; it loses its last letter

explanation.surface: A jazz critic holds on to security, along with a poem by the puzzle's poet.
explanation.walkthrough: 26 is AN ODE and 10 is JOHN KEATS, so '26 by 10' is a Keats ode; this one is the Ode on Melancholy.
explanation.definitionFit: Keats wrote the Ode on Melancholy, so this sad mood is the topic of one of his famous odes.

clue.text: See 24

definitions.note: a cross-reference rather than a definition: this light holds the second half of the phrase clued at 24 down, which means the while

blocks.note: the clue at 24 down reads as me anti me; the tail of anti and the second me land in this light

explanation.walkthrough: This light finishes the answer begun at 24 down, whose clue 'I'm my own enemy the while' reads as me anti me, a phrase meaning the while.
explanation.definitionFit: Together with 24 down this light completes a phrase meaning the interval while something else happens.

clue.text: Nasty French article left in keeping of farm worker

indicators.note: something in someone's keeping is held by them, so it sits inside

blocks.note: un is the French for 'a'
a peasant works the land
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A nasty French newspaper item was left with a farmhand.
explanation.definitionFit: Unpleasant means disagreeable or offensive, which is what nasty means.

clue.text: Dark and windy 12 with 26 by 10

definitions.note: the subject of Keats's Ode to a Nightingale

blocks.note: night is the dark part of the day
12 is TIME, and a windy time is one spent in a gale

explanation.surface: A dark, windy night is paired with a poem by the puzzle's poet.
explanation.walkthrough: 12 across is TIME; a windy time is read as a spell 'in gale'. '26 by 10' is a Keats ode, here Ode to a Nightingale.
explanation.definitionFit: Keats wrote his Ode to a Nightingale about the songbird he heard in a Hampstead garden.

clue.text: SOS - erring characters of Scots family include John, the film director

definitions.text: Scots family include John, the film director

indicators.note: erring means straying from the right path, so the letters wander

blocks.note: taken as written
the indicator word also supplies its own letters
surface padding: the letters are the characters being mixed

explanation.surface: A distress call goes out about wandering Scots, including a film-maker called John.
explanation.walkthrough: 'erring' does double duty: its letters are part of the mix and it also signals the mix. John Grierson was the Scottish pioneer of documentary film.
explanation.definitionFit: John Grierson, the Scottish documentary maker, belonged to this family, so its members are the Griersons.

clue.text: 10's girl took ale with basil - potty!

indicators.note: potty means crazy, so the letters go mad; it also hints at a pot

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A girl had ale with herbs and went a bit mad.
explanation.walkthrough: 10 is John Keats, whose poem Isabella, or the Pot of Basil has the heroine keep her murdered lover's head in a basil pot; 'potty' is a pun on it.
explanation.definitionFit: Isabella is the heroine of Keats's narrative poem about the pot of basil.

clue.text: 26 by 10, girl who growed to a revolutionary

definitions.note: a noun phrase standing for the poem, fair because the entry is the phrase that follows the word Ode in the poem's title

blocks.note: Topsy in Uncle Tom's Cabin says she was never born but 'just growed'
Che Guevara, the Argentine-born revolutionary

explanation.surface: A poem, a self-made girl and a revolutionary are lined up together.
explanation.walkthrough: '26 by 10' is a Keats ode; this one is the Ode to Psyche, so the entry is the two-word phrase after 'Ode'.
explanation.definitionFit: Keats addressed one ode to Psyche, so the phrase completes its title after the word Ode.

clue.text: Cone, perhaps, Amos left tied up with string

indicators.note: things tied up are knotted and twisted out of their order

blocks.note: taken as written
L is the abbreviation for left
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cone left by a man called Amos is bound up in string.
explanation.walkthrough: A storm cone is a canvas cone hoisted at British ports to warn ships of gales, so 'perhaps' marks it as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: A storm cone is one kind of warning hoisted on shore to tell shipping of an approaching gale.

clue.text: Sound of Business Guardian's jokes

blocks.note: a hum is the low sound of busy activity
the newspaper speaking of itself says 'our'

explanation.surface: The business pages of the Guardian are said to carry some jokes.
explanation.walkthrough: The sound is the hum of business; the Guardian, in which the puzzle appeared, refers to its own things as 'our'.
explanation.definitionFit: Humour is the quality of being funny, as found in jokes and comic writing.

clue.text: Show your face and turn victorious day into nothing

indicators.note: putting one thing into another places it inside

blocks.note: a U is a turn, as in a U-turn
nil means nothing
VE Day was Victory in Europe Day, 8 May 1945

explanation.surface: Someone takes off a mask and makes a triumphant day come to nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: To unveil is to take the covering off, so to show your face is to remove a veil.

clue.text: First lady's man to get transport to hospital

blocks.note: a bus is public transport
H is the map abbreviation for hospital

explanation.surface: The President is to be taken to hospital, transport arranged.
explanation.walkthrough: The First Lady is the US President's wife, so her man is the President himself; the clue dates from 2001, when Laura Bush held the title.
explanation.definitionFit: George W. Bush was married to Laura Bush, who was First Lady while he was President.

clue.text: Straight nose with run off for 26 by 10

definitions.note: the subject of Keats's Ode on a Grecian Urn

indicators.note: something gone off has spoiled, so the word is no longer in its proper form

blocks.note: a Grecian nose runs in a straight line from the forehead
taken as written

explanation.surface: A runny nose is out of the way, with a poem by the puzzle's poet to follow.
explanation.walkthrough: '26 by 10' is a Keats ode, this time the Ode on a Grecian Urn.
explanation.definitionFit: Keats wrote his Ode on a Grecian Urn about a painted vase from ancient Greece.

clue.text: Actors heard at religious level

indicators.note: heard tells us to go by what reaches the ear, not the spelling

blocks.note: the actors in a play are its cast

explanation.surface: Performers are listened to at a religious gathering of some rank.
explanation.walkthrough: The Hindu social order is divided into hereditary ranks, which is why the definition calls it religious.
explanation.definitionFit: A caste is a hereditary rank in the Hindu social hierarchy, a level fixed by religion.

clue.text: I'm my own enemy the while

definitions.note: it defines the whole phrase made by this light and 12 across together, MEAN plus TIME, which means the while

blocks.note: the speaker, the first person
an enemy is anti, against; its first two letters end this light and the rest runs on into 12 across
the speaker again, me; these letters land in 12 across

explanation.surface: Someone confesses to being their own worst enemy for a while.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs over two lights, 24 down then 12 across. Being one's own enemy is being 'me anti me', the speaker set against the speaker.
explanation.definitionFit: The meantime is the interval while something else goes on, so the phrase means the while.

clue.text: Don Juan-type hero among disguised clues

indicators.note: a disguised thing is altered so its appearance is changed
to be among others is to sit in the middle of them

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A Don Juan figure, the hero of the story, moves among clues that are in disguise.
explanation.walkthrough: Don Juan is the legendary seducer, so a Don Juan type is lustful; the definition is adjectival.
explanation.definitionFit: Don Juan is the byword for a womaniser, so a man of his type is lustful and lewd.

clue.text: A swelling destination for electrons

blocks.note: taken as written
a node is a knob or swelling, as on a joint or a plant stem

explanation.surface: A swelling seems to be where electrons are heading.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as two words it is also 'an ode', which is why other clues use '26 by 10' for a Keats ode.
explanation.definitionFit: Electrons flow in a circuit towards the positive electrode, which attracts them.

clue.text: Declare seamen to be in low water?

blocks.note: to aver is to declare firmly
the NUS was the National Union of Seamen

explanation.surface: Sailors announce that they are in shallow water.
explanation.walkthrough: Avernus is a crater lake near Naples which the ancients took for the entrance to the underworld, so its water is 'low' in the sense of lower world.
explanation.definitionFit: The lake was believed to lead down to Hades, making it water belonging to the lower regions.

clue.text: Fascinate non-standard parent with time for other things

indicators.note: 'non' tells us to remove the word for a standard, written par in golf, from what follows

blocks.note: the word parent without its first three letters
hr is the abbreviation for hour
al. is short for the Latin alia, as in et al., and others

explanation.surface: A parent with an unusual way of life makes time for other interests.
explanation.walkthrough: PAR is the standard score in golf, so a 'non-standard parent' is the word with PAR taken away.
explanation.definitionFit: To enthral someone is to hold their attention spellbound, which is to fascinate them.
